assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Rate constant
items.clue: The proportionality factor, k; it changes with temperature but not with concentration.

items.label: Second order
items.clue: Rate against concentration curves upward ever more steeply; each halving takes longer.

items.label: Calibration graph
items.clue: Straight-line plot of readings against concentration, from which an unknown is read off.

items.label: Activation energy
items.clue: On a profile, the height from the reactants up to the top of the barrier; always positive.

questions.stem: A student uses a colorimeter to find the concentration of a blue solution of copper(II) sulfate. Which filter should the student use, and why?

options.text: A blue filter, because the solution is blue.
An orange filter, because the solution absorbs orange light strongly.
No filter, because white light contains every colour and gives the largest reading.
Any filter, because absorbance depends only on the concentration.

questions.explanation: Orange is the colour the blue solution absorbs most. Absorbance at that colour changes most with concentration, so the readings are most sensitive.

questions.stem: Which energy profile correctly shows an endothermic reaction?

options.text: Products higher than reactants; Ea arrow from the reactants up to the peak; ΔH arrow from reactants up to products.
Products higher than reactants; Ea arrow from the products up to the peak.
Products lower than reactants; ΔH arrow pointing down; Ea arrow from reactants up to the peak.
Products higher than reactants; Ea arrow from the reactants up to the products level.

questions.explanation: Endothermic means products are higher in energy. Ea runs from the reactants to the top of the barrier; ΔH from reactants to products.

questions.stem: The rate equation for a reaction is rate = k[A]², with concentrations in mol dm⁻³ and the rate in mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. What are the units of k?

options.text: mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹, as the rate constant has the same units as the rate
mol⁻¹ dm³ s⁻¹, as k = rate/[A]² for a second-order reaction
s⁻¹, as only one reactant, A, appears in the rate equation
mol³ dm⁻⁹ s⁻¹, as k = rate × [A]² when the rate equation is rearranged

questions.explanation: (mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹)/(mol dm⁻³)² = mol⁻¹ dm³ s⁻¹, for any reaction that is second order overall.

questions.stem: In an iodine clock, the blue-black colour appears after 48 s. A second run uses double the concentration of I⁻, with everything else the same, and the colour appears after 24 s. What is the order with respect to I⁻?

options.text: Zero order, as the same amount of iodine forms in both runs.
Order −1, as the time halves when [I⁻] doubles.
Second order, as [I⁻] doubles and the time halves: a factor of 2 × 2.
First order, as 1/t doubles when [I⁻] doubles.

questions.explanation: Rate ∝ 1/t. Doubling [I⁻] doubles 1/t, so the rate is proportional to [I⁻]: first order.

questions.stem: A green solution of nickel(II) ions is taken from a lab waste container. Its absorbance is measured under the same conditions as these nickel(II) standards. Standards (mol dm⁻³ : A): 0.050 : 0.16 · 0.100 : 0.32 · 0.150 : 0.48 · 0.200 : 0.64. The sample gives A = 0.40. What is its nickel(II) concentration, in mol dm⁻³?
questions.explanation: The points lie on a straight line through the origin: A = 3.2 × c. So c = 0.40 ÷ 3.2 = 0.125. Reading across from A = 0.40 to the line gives the same value.

questions.stem: A mixture of hydrogen and oxygen can stay unchanged at room temperature for years. In Döbereiner's lamp (1823), a jet of hydrogen in air strikes a piece of platinum and reacts at once, with no flame or spark to start it. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: The platinum heats the gas, so the curve moves to higher energy and more molecules exceed the same Ea.
The platinum gives a route with a lower Ea, so at the same temperature far more molecules have enough energy.
The platinum makes the reaction more exothermic, so the molecules gain the energy they need to react.
The platinum changes the shape of the curve, moving its peak to higher energy without heating.

questions.stem: The rate equation for a reaction is rate = k[A][B]². At constant temperature, the concentrations of A and B are both doubled. By what factor does the rate increase?
questions.explanation: Doubling [A] gives ×2¹ = 2; doubling [B] gives ×2² = 4. The rate rises by 2 × 4 = 8.

questions.stem: A hypothetical compound X decomposes at constant temperature. Three runs give these initial rates. - [X] / mol dm⁻³: 0.160, 0.320, 0.640. Initial rate / mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹: 5.60 × 10⁻⁴, 1.12 × 10⁻³, 2.24 × 10⁻³. - What are the order with respect to X and the rate constant, k?

options.text: Second order; k = 2.19 × 10⁻² dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹
First order; k = 2.86 × 10² s
First order; k = 3.50 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹
First order; k = 3.50 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹

questions.explanation: Rate ×2 when [X] ×2: first order. k = 5.60 × 10⁻⁴ ÷ 0.160 = 3.50 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ (same from every run).

questions.stem: Which reaction is best followed by colorimetry?

options.text: Magnesium ribbon with dilute hydrochloric acid
Calcium carbonate chips with dilute hydrochloric acid
Hydrogen peroxide with acidified potassium iodide
Ethyl ethanoate with sodium hydroxide solution

questions.explanation: H₂O₂ + 2I⁻ + 2H⁺ → I₂ + 2H₂O. The reactants are colourless and iodine forms, turning the mixture yellow-brown. Absorbance rises as [I₂] rises, measured continuously with no gas lost or samples taken.
